title: Positional obstructive sleep apnea in children prescribed continuous positive airway pressure therapy for obstructive sleep‐disordered breathing

sections.abstract: Positional obstructive sleep apnea, in which there is a ≥ 2:1 predominance of obstructive events in the supine position, is a sleep‐disordered breathing phenotype with a targeted treatment in the form of positional device therapy. We sought to determine the prevalence of positional obstructive sleep apnea in a cohort of children prescribed continuous positive airway pressure therapy, ascertain risk factors for the condition, and determine the associated continuous positive airway pressure treatment adherence rate. A retrospective cohort study of all children > 2 years old from a single tertiary paediatric centre prescribed continuous positive airway pressure therapy over an 8‐year period was conducted. Positional obstructive sleep apnea prevalence was established by analysing positional and respiratory event data from the participants' original diagnostic polysomnography. Continuous positive airway pressure therapy adherence was determined using data from machine download. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression modelling was used to determine participant demographic and clinical factors associated with positional obstruction. Positional obstructive sleep apnea (defined by Bignold's criteria modified for paediatric use) prevalence in the cohort of 237 analysed participants was 38%. Suboptimal continuous positive airway pressure adherence was noted in 30% of this group based on initial machine download, performed a median of 96 days post‐treatment initiation. Higher age and lower obstructive apnea–hypopnea index were independent predictors of positional obstructive sleep apnea, whereas neurodevelopmental diagnosis, presence/absence of rapid eye movement‐related obstructive sleep apnea, overweight/obesity status and history of adenoidectomy/adenotonsillectomy were not. For children, positional device therapy is a treatment option worthy of further consideration and research.
sections.introduction:
Positional obstructive sleep apnea (POSA), sleep‐disordered breathing with a predominance of obstructive events in the supine sleep position, is a sleep apnea phenotype with a targeted treatment in the form of positional device therapy (de Vries et al., 2015 ). In patients with POSA, the tongue and other tissues of the upper airway may collapse backward while in the supine position, narrowing the airway and increasing resistance (Landry et al., 2023 ). Lateral or prone positioning reduces this airway collapse, thereby reducing obstruction. For adults, recent guidelines (Randerath et al., 2021 ) and trial meta‐analyses (ALQarni et al., 2023 ; Ravesloot et al., 2017 ) suggest positional devices are a suitable alternative to continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for treating POSA. Whilst POSA is reportedly the most common clinical and physiological phenotype recognisable in adults (Landry et al., 2023 ), there are fewer reports of its prevalence in children, and none focussing on the group of children prescribed CPAP, a cohort in which targeted POSA treatments may prove to be a useful alternative.

In children, focussing upon POSA, reports of prevalence vary from 18% to 58%, depending on the particular population studied (Selvadurai et al., 2020 ; Verhelst et al., 2019 ; Wu et al., 2022 ). Some evidence has shown that children with an increased risk of anatomical obstruction (such as those with Trisomy 21 who have multifactorial aetiology for their obstructive sleep apnea [OSA]) instinctively adopt sleep positions that optimise airflow and mitigate the risk of apnea (Santoro et al., 2021 ); this instinctively‐adopted positional solution for OSA in children suggests therefore that actively initiating POSA therapy may be of benefit in subgroups of children with OSA. Only a single pilot study, using positioning pillows, has explored this concept as a treatment for paediatric POSA, but did demonstrate an improvement in OSA with the therapy (Xiao et al., 2021 ).

First‐line therapy for paediatric OSA is adenotonsillectomy, which is curative for more than half of patients (Lee et al., 2016 ). However, a significant number of children have residual OSA, warranting additional treatment; CPAP is a common second‐line option that nevertheless comes with challenges in establishing and sustaining adherence, reflected by adherence rates varying by centre and subpopulation, but overall approaching 50% (Sawunyavisuth et al., 2023 ). We therefore sought to explore whether a subgroup of children who are prescribed CPAP may be suited to an alternative POSA‐targeting therapy, should further research prove efficacy of this treatment paradigm for children as demonstrated in adults. The specific aim of our study was therefore to determine the prevalence of POSA in children prescribed CPAP in our tertiary centre, and explore its association with CPAP adherence, to ascertain whether resources should be allocated to establishing a supported pathway for trialling positional device therapy for selected patients.
sections.methods:
This was a retrospective cohort study of all children prescribed CPAP for OSA at Queensland Children's Hospital (QCH) between January 2015 and January 2023. QCH human research ethics exemption was obtained (HREC reference EX/2024/QCHQ/107075). We excluded children prescribed CPAP for reasons other than OSA (e.g. severe lung disease), and children who did not have a complete diagnostic polysomnography (PSG) at QCH prior to CPAP initiation. Relevant PSG variables from the Level 1 diagnostic study performed prior to CPAP prescription (i.e. from the PSG in which the diagnosis of OSA was made) were extracted, including obstructive apnea–hypopnoea index (OAHI) in supine and non‐supine positions, further subdivided into rapid eye movement (REM) and non‐REM sleep periods in these positions. PSG was undertaken using N7000 signal acquisition hardware with RemLogic 3.4.1 (Natus Medical). Sleep staging and event scoring was performed in accordance with the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM, Darien, IL, USA) guidelines relevant and applicable at the time of the PSG. In our centre during the time period 1 January 2020–1 January 2022, the patient's initial sleep position, and any subsequent changes to sleep position, was routinely recorded by manual electronic entry into the PSG acquisition software by the attending sleep nurse, and was also recorded with a position sensor calibrated at the start of recording. For 12 PSG recordings in which sleep time was noted without a nurse‐verified patient position or in‐range and valid position sensor output, saved data were opened and manual review of the PSG (including video) recording was undertaken by a senior sleep scientist to code patient position correctly. For the period 1 January 2015–31 December 2019, position was manually entered by the attending sleep nurse, with some variability in completion of this task. Therefore, all PSGs from this period were reviewed by a medical student using the accompanying video recording and patient position re‐entered into the software; the student received prior instruction and viewed examples of the various sleep positions, with any uncertain periods reviewed by a paediatric sleep physician or scientist.

The POSA was defined and prevalence reported according to Cartwright's (Cartwright, 1984 ), Bignold's (Bignold et al., 2011 ) and Amsterdam positional OSA (APOC; Frank et al., 2015 ) criteria, with modification made to these (specified in Table 1 ) to account for differences between adult and paediatric OSA. Bignold's criteria specify a clearly‐defined period of time (minimum 20 min) in both supine and non‐supine sleep as a requirement for POSA diagnosis. Given this definition was practical and clinically useful in previous paediatric research (Selvadurai et al., 2020 ), it was utilised for subgroup analysis.

Prevalence of POSA and associated rates of CPAP adherence.

APOC, Amsterdam positional obstructive sleep apnea; CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure; POSA, positional obstructive sleep apnea.

Cartwright's criterion (modified): supine to non‐supine OAHI ratio ≥ 2.

Bignold's criteria (modified): supine to non‐supine OAHI ratio ≥ 2, and at least 20 min of time in both supine and non‐supine sleep positions.

APOC criteria (modified): supine to non‐supine OAHI ratio ≥ 2, and at least 10% of time in both supine and non‐supine sleep positions.

As OSA is a REM‐predominant disease in children (Katz & D'Ambrosio, 2008 ), we also reported the prevalence of REM OSA in our cohort. Paediatric REM OSA was defined as previously described; REM OAHI was more than double the non‐REM OAHI (Wu et al., 2022 ). We explored the interaction between REM OSA and POSA by reporting upon the change in REM‐related obstruction from supine to non‐supine position for those children meeting criteria for both REM OSA and POSA. Patient demographic, anthropometric and clinical information was also collated, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI) category (normal weight, overweight, obese), neurodevelopmental or syndromic diagnosis, prior adenoidectomy ± tonsillectomy, and days from CPAP commencement to the first machine download. Information on race/ethnicity was not available. CPAP adherence data from the first machine download after CPAP initiation were also included, with CPAP adherence being defined as meeting ≥ 70% nightly usage with on average ≥ 4 hr usage on nights used.

Pearson's chi‐squared tests and Mann–Whitney U ‐tests were used to compare POSA and non‐POSA groups for categorical and continuous variables, respectively, and univariable logistic regression analysis was used to determine factors associated with POSA. Variables with p < 0.2 for any level or that changed estimates of the association of interest by 10% were included in multivariable modelling. Stata 17 (StataCorp, LLC) was utilised for all statistical analysis; two‐tailed p ‐values of < 0.05 were considered significant.
sections.results:
Over the study period, 376 children underwent CPAP initiation at QCH. Seventeen children were excluded as they were aged < 2 years at the time of their diagnostic PSG, 13 were excluded as CPAP was prescribed for a non‐OSA indication, and 109 were excluded as they did not have a full diagnostic PSG at QCH prior to CPAP initiation (either because CPAP was commenced prior to completion of the full night of diagnostic analysis, or because they were referred in for CPAP initiation from another centre that had performed the diagnostic study). A total of 237 children were therefore included in this analysis (Figure 1 ).

Patient inclusion flow diagram. CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure; OSA, obstructive sleep apnea; QCH, Queensland Children's Hospital; PSG, polysomnography.

Eighty‐eight (37%) included participants were female, and the median age across all participants was 12 years (interquartile range [IQR] 8–14 years; Table 2 ). Forty‐nine (21%) patients had mild OSA, 52 (22%) had moderate OSA (OAHI of 5–10 per hr) and 136 patients (57%) had severe OSA (OAHI ≥ 10 per hr). Twenty‐four (10%) participants were overweight (BMI within the 85th–95th centile), and 137 (59%) were obese (BMI > 95th centile) at their PSG. Seventy‐seven (32%) had a significant neurodevelopmental or syndromic diagnosis, 155 (65%) had previously undergone adenoidectomy with or without tonsillectomy, and 89 (38%) met criteria for REM OSA. Demographic and clinical features across modified Bignold's criterion‐defined POSA and non‐POSA groups are shown in Table 2 .

Demographic, anthropometric and clinical features of the patient population across POSA and non‐POSA groups.

CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure; IQR, interquartile range; OSA, obstructive sleep apnea; POSA, positional obstructive sleep apnea; REM, rapid eye movement.

p ‐values computed using Pearson's χ 2 ‐test.

p ‐values computed using the Mann–Whitney U ‐test.

The prevalence of POSA varied between 36% and 57% depending on definition used, with the rate of CPAP adherence for those with POSA 70%–74% (Table 1 ). Univariable and multivariable modelling showed greater age and lower OAHI were significantly associated with POSA (defined by modified Bignold's criteria), including independently of one another, while previous ENT surgery, neurodevelopmental diagnosis, overweight/obesity status and REM OSA status did not significantly interact with POSA diagnosis (Table 3 ). The relationship between: (a) age; and (b) OAHI with supine to non‐supine ratio is shown in Figures 2 and 3 , respectively.

Supine to non‐supine obstructive apnea–hypopnea index (OAHI) ratio as it relates to OAHI. Grey dashed line indicates a supine/non‐supine (S/NS) OAHI ratio of 2. Crosses above or below box and whisker plots represent outliers.

Out of the 33 children who met criteria for both POSA (established by modified Bignold's criteria) and REM OSA, 67% ( n = 22) had ≥ 20 min of supine REM and non‐supine REM sleep; nearly all of these (21/22) were found to have during supine REM sleep an OAHI more than double that seen during non‐supine REM sleep. About half ( n = 45, 51%) of the 89 children with REM OSA in our cohort did not, however, have ≥ 20 min of both supine and non‐supine REM sleep observed in their diagnostic PSG, so the supine to non‐supine REM OAHI ratio could not be determined for them.
sections.discussion:
This retrospective cohort study is the first to examine the prevalence of POSA in a cohort of children prescribed CPAP for obstructive sleep‐disordered breathing, and provides important key findings to guide clinical practice and future research focus.

Our study found that more than a quarter of those with POSA had suboptimal CPAP use based on their initial machine download. This therefore identifies a group of children in whom treatment of OSA with current standard therapies is suboptimal, and suggests that positional therapy may lower the overall burden of OSA in these children. This is further supported by the emerging evidence that positional devices are better tolerated than CPAP by adult patients, with high patient satisfaction rates (Hidalgo‐Armas et al., 2023 ). To explore this further, prospective study of different positional device treatments is warranted in a cohort of children with POSA, and should include the acceptability of such therapy to children and their families.

As there is no single widely‐accepted definition of paediatric POSA and those developed for adults are not suitable for children, in our study we utilised multiple POSA definitions, altering them only to make them applicable to children. Bignold's and APOC criteria have total AHI‐related components and thresholds not utilised for this study, as paediatric OSA definitions and severity cut‐offs differ from adult OSA (Verhelst et al., 2019 ). Paediatric OSA is better categorised using the OAHI, as specified by international guidelines (Chamnanpet et al., 2022 ; Kaditis et al., 2017 ), so we altered POSA definitions to use this metric instead of the AHI, noting that other paediatric studies also utilised this approach (Selvadurai et al., 2020 ; Verhelst et al., 2019 ). Working toward a consensus definition of paediatric POSA may be useful for future research efforts.

An additional consideration explored in this study is the interaction between REM OSA and POSA. This is relevant as a patient who has obstructive events predominantly in REM sleep, with REM sleep occurring in the supine position during their PSG but not occurring in another sleep position, could be labelled as having POSA even if therapy to alter their sleep position might not greatly improve their OSA if it persists to the same degree in REM sleep regardless of position. However, it appears that children with REM‐predominant obstruction actually have similar or greater improvement in their obstruction with moving out of the supine position. Out of 22 children with both POSA and REM OSA who additionally had ≥ 20 min REM sleep periods in both supine and non‐supine positions, 95% ( n = 21) had a ≥ 50% decline in the number of obstructive events in the non‐supine position. This suggests that children with POSA who have REM‐predominant obstruction are still likely to improve their OSA with successful positional therapy. Whilst a limitation of our study is that the number of patients from which this conclusion is drawn is small, the finding is consistent with previous similar research (Hidalgo‐Armas et al., 2023 ). It may be beneficial to attempt to reposition patients with REM OSA who are potential candidates for POSA treatment during their PSG to capture sufficient REM sleep in different positions, to better understand how positional device therapy might or might not benefit them.

A limitation of our study is its single‐centre nature. The prevalence of POSA in our population using the modified Bignold's definition (38%) differs from that reported using the same definition in a group of obese 8–18‐year‐old children (58%; Sawunyavisuth et al., 2023 ). This difference may arise due to the different population characteristics, as the current study includes non‐obese children with a wider age range, but focuses only on those prescribed CPAP for their OSA. Furthermore, severity bias may have influenced our findings, as children prescribed with CPAP represent a more severe subset of patients with OSA, thus overestimating the prevalence and impact of POSA. Selection bias could also arise as children without a complete diagnostic PSG or those referred from external centres were excluded, thus limiting generalisability. Bias could also arise from variations in how sleep position was recorded or validated during PSGs, affecting the accuracy of POSA classification.

Age and obesity were found to be independent predictors of POSA in one paediatric study (Verhelst et al., 2019 ), but these findings have not been consistently replicated in other similar analyses (Selvadurai et al., 2020 ; Wu et al., 2022 ), including our own. However, the overall prevalence of REM OSA in our population (38%) is similar to the 43%–50% reported in other paediatric research (Chamnanpet et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2022 ).

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that approximately two in five children prescribed CPAP for obstructive sleep‐disordered breathing have POSA, and that 30% of them are non‐adherent to CPAP. Given the recognised challenges with CPAP therapy in children and the paucity of non‐invasive alternatives, further prospective paediatric trials assessing the efficacy of and longer‐term adherence to positional devices are essential to optimise management options for OSA in paediatric patients.
